I added the 94-page "ZGRASS Paint Program Users Guide" to Bally Alley.
This is the March 12, 1982, Preliminary Version.  I'm not sure if there is a later version, but this is what is available to me.

Here is what is written in the "About This Guide:"

You are about to experience an interactive painting system that will enable you to immensely expand your creative drawing and image development capabilities. With the help of this guide, you'll find the system simple to use and rich in capabilities.

The Zgrass PAINT PROGRAM USER'S GUIDE has been designed to guide you through an interactive experience with all modules of the Paint Program in a sequence which will prepare you to use each module as you encounter it. If you take the time now to experiment with the Paint Program system as instructed in this guide, you'll minimize the amount of time you spend learning how to use the system to maximum capacity. If you are a neophyte in the world of computers, you'll find this a pleasant and relatively painless introduction to working with computers.

In general, this guide is set up to be followed in a step-by-step manner, explaining what's happening as you engage in new activities in each module. As you become more comfortable with the controls and various means of interacting with the system, you may find repetitive instructions tedious or boring. On the other hand, if you're shaking in your boots because it's the first time you've dealt with a computer, you'll probably find the repetition comforting. To minimize the amount of repetition, those concepts or activities which come into play frequently or require special explanation have been presented in the GENERAL REFERENCE SECTION of this guide and are referred to accordingly within the body of the guide.

Sections of this document include:

1 - Getting Started
2 - General Reference Section
3 - Group - 1) Basic Drawing Brushes
4 - Group - 2) Colormap Selection & Storage
5 - Group - 3) Making & Using Snaps
6 - Group - 4) Line & Snap Animation
7 - Group - 5) Utility Modules

This document has been been bookmarked in Acrobat for ease of reading.

You can view the guide here:

http://tinyurl.com/degp4u

http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/zgrass/zgrass_docs/ZGRASS_Paint_Program_Users_Guide.pdf

Enjoy!

7251:
I modified the ZGRASS Lessons Manual manual already online by adding the cover page and lesson 0 that Paul scanned in.  This 52-page is from October 27, 1981.  Here is what the Read Me First says:

Zgrass is a graphics programming language. It is probably closer to BASIC than any other language, yet it is much more flexible and general than BASIC. The presumption in these lessons is that you already know how to program BASIC (at least BALLY BASIC) and are familiar with loops, IF's, GOTO's, variables, and so on, and are ready to learn what makes Zgrass tick. The essential differences between Zgrass and BASIC are:

1. Zgrass allows any number of programs and subroutines, each named, and they can run in series or parallel. BASIC has one unnamed program
and a lot of GOSUB's.

2. Zgrass has an interactive full-screen editor. BASIC edits with line numbers.

3. Zgrass has good ways of passing arguments to subroutines; BASIC has none.

4. Zgrass can construct programs and run them with string manipulation features; BASIC cannot.

5. Zgrass has excellent debugging aids: single step, run-time listing, and error trapping; BASIC doesn't.

6. Zgrass has fast, advanced graphics commands; most BASICs use peek and poke.

7. BASIC has FOR/NEXT. Zgrass does without.

In order to learn Zgrass, you will have to explore it. Fortunately, this is not hard and is very rewarding. These lessons are to help you start exploring. They don't teach you how to program or write games, they just present the tools to you and encourage you to build your own. The first six lessons concentrate on defining the playing field. Pay close attention!

If you find a word being used that you do not understand, consult the Glossary. Once you get through the lessons, read the Glossary in detail. You'll find yourself understanding some of the esoterica. Some of the advanced features you may never use or understand and it may take awhile for you to see why  some of the diversions from BASIC were necessary. Before long, however, you will find going back to BASIC unbearable.

Just to get you started, there's a test program called NB in the system. Press the red RST on the UV-1 front panel and answer Y. Then type the two letters NB and press the RETURN key. An image will appear. Type NB and press RETURN again. The image will undo itself. For more action, type NB.B and press RETURN. You can stop this by pressing the CTRL (called CONTROL on some keyboards) key, holding it down and simultaneously pressing the C key. Have fun!

All Lessons:

0 - Read Me First
1 - Getting Started
2 - Writing Macros
3 - Editing
4 - More on Macros
5 - Storing Macros on Tape and Disk
6 - Debugging
7 - Device Variables and Ports
8 - Arrays
9 - More on Graphics
10 - Swap Modules
11 - Advanced Concepts

You can read the ZGRASS Lessons Manual here:

http://tinyurl.com/cst7ec

(or use the full URL:)

http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/zgrass/zgrass_docs/ZGRASS_Lessons_Manual.pdf

Enjoy!

Hey everyone,

I'm a soon-to-be new Bally Astrocade owner , just waiting for my unit to ship out, and in the meantime I've been reading the FAQ documents at BallyAlley. I'm concerned about the over-heating warning, and I have a few questions related to some of the suggestions, and I'd also like to hear other suggestions on what folks do to keep their units from overheating.

Putting the Astrocade on a hard surface: I plan on playing the unit while it's on top of one of those fold-up TV dinner tables since it'll allow me to keep it close by in case I need to interact with the console during gameplay. Is this a good enough surface to place it on to keep it form over heating?Placing the Astrocade on top of an empty box: I'm having a bit of a hard time envisioning this, so I'd love to hear from people who've tried this. What I'm envisioning, is that I'd get an empty box and seal it up so there are no flaps hanging out and so the unit doesn't sink in. How does placing the unit on an empty box help exactly? I'm assuming because it's more ventilated than just a regular hard surface? 

Adam answered my question on adding on larger cushion feet from Radio Shack so I don't need to pose that one here.  I look forward to hearing your responses!

Thanks,
Jose
7258:
I have mine on a box.  The system has two vent areas--on the left side of the bottom and the right side of the bottom.  I found a fairly short, thin, sturdy box, and centered the system on top of it so that the sides hung over the box a bit.  Now, there's no surface to obstruct the vents.  I haven't had any problems using the system like this, even typing on the keypad.  There's really nothing special about the box.  It could just as well be a wooden block.  Raising the feet up would have about the same effect.

Paul

7259:
Jose wrote:
>>
I had a question on some of the suggestions on the over-heating problem.
>>

For the record, I've answered this question in a private email, but I thought that it would be worthwhile to post my comments on the board:

Here's what I've done with my Astrocade to keep the heat down:

1) Rubber Feet.  I don't recall if I had to remove original feet or not.  I don't THINK so.

2) Removed Internal Shielding.  This actually required some desolding.

3) I used my Astrocade with the top off.

4) If I'm going to use my Astrocade for LONG time (say, if I'm programming it), then I actually put a fan on it to blow across the chips.  This is probably overkill.

I've never used the box method.

Adam

situation.

people put their Astrocade on top of boxes.  I'm certainly
not the only one thinking about the life expectancy of their
little Astrocade!

7277:
Jose Monzon wrote:

> Is there a step-by-step guide somewhere on how to remove the RF > shielding? It seems that on some units there is shielding both above the > motherboard, and underneath that needs to be removed. How long did it > take people to remove the shielding from their units?
> > Thank you Lance, for posting the pictures of the different Astrocade > shielding, it helped give me an idea of what I'm in for. Looks a bit > complex but it might just be my inexperience talking. :) > To remove shielding:

1) Remove six screws from bottom of arcade unit.

2) Turn unit over and lift top half off.

3) Remove metal pinch clips from around shielding edges.

4) If unit has 1/2 top plate with heat bar, lift up and snap off or de-solder from bottom back shielding. (Can be lifted and replaced if you just want temporary access to main board.)

5) locate screws that mount main board to bottom chassis (Usually slotted hex head) Remove and store.

6) lift and slide RF unit out to the left.

6A) If unit has newer shielding, remove the smaller screws holding main board to shield. Lift main board and remove bottom plate.

6B) If unit had full plate top shield, (Plastic or otherwise) lift board and turn over. Remove the big screws holding the cart/number bas assembly in place. Gently tilt up assembly arround the cart port and slide off the number pad board.

6B2) Push the pinch rivets out of there holes, this releases the layers of paper board et all on the bottom of the main board.

Full top plate can now be discarded. Bottom plate also.


To remount main board without shielding:

1) If cart/numberpad assembly was removed gently slide pad board along guides into the assembly. Must reach stops. Gently tilt down around the cart port and screw into place.

2) Place main board over posts.(may have to align ports edge and rotate down.) screw into place.

3) Slide RF unit onto pins and press gently down into place.

4) Replace top of unit, turn over and restore screws.


You may add a heat sink to the DATA chip before reassembly, Its the one with the metal on or above it. nearest the RF unit.

This is all off the top of my head, there may be minor errors.

Lance

Sigh...

What can I say? Well... That my eyes were bigger than my stomach when we started?
:-)

The yellow sheet with Snoopy (don't ask) was the first 'concept' drawing. This was late 1982, around Halloween (Snoopy in a mask, still don't ask...). The sea floor was going to be much more interesting originally. But resolution, time, and code space all were factors that led to the final game... Yea, I even wanted clouds... sigh.

We made Arcade 'graph paper' and printed up in pads to help our development. I still have some left. This made designing to scale easier.

The 'next' concept drawing was the one with the orange boat on the top left and the yellow submarine and the octopus with the note that says, "drifts towards diver". Unfortunately, that made the game rather hard, so we just had the octopus go back and forth on the bottom... You may notice that there was still a lot of area devoted to the sea bottom. That too made the game hard to play, so I flattened the sea bottom out a bit.

The next drawing was just to get a better idea of the play area. This was the orange sea bottom, green sea and blue sky drawing. Notice the 'waves' and spray at the top of the ocean. Great game idea, but it made the boat look weird, so we ended up with a flat sea. And the ocean bottom was still too difficult to work with... so...

The next concept, and the one that I based the game on, was the screen with the OXY indicator, and the drawing of the "Calypso" ship. (I always wanted to do the Calypso as the ship...) That was mid-December.

As this process was going on, Marion had offered some ideas for the game. These were the sheets with the boat that has the note "Have treasures appear on ledge and boat" and the sheet labeled "Diver Down". I liked Marion's diver animation, but we did not have the ROM space for all the animations. And while his sub was fine, I wanted to put the "Yellow Submarine" into the game... yea, Beatle's fan ;-)

I also liked Marion's idea to have a larger than one screen scrolling view for the game, but that was not practical then (I might be able to do that now with some time and more thinking).

I started to map out some ideas for graphics in the game. The sheet with the torpedo, treasure chest and pirate flag came next. I remember trying to work out the angle on drawing an anchor. Harder than you think in low resolution... Also you see the first try at the sunken ship that eventually made it onto the splash screen. And you can see a brown 'script' "T" that I worked out that I wanted to have a script text of "Treasure Cove". But again, since this was a large graphic (and not text), I had to default back to the standard text because I did not have the code space for a large graphic title.

Various sheets of fish, diver and other graphics were worked on. I remember trying to draw the Calypso in a 35 pixel width. Not easy and still have it look like the Calypso.
http://www.sealetter.com/news/photos/calypso.jpg

The second to last screen is actually labeled "Final Title Screen". But the top screen is actually the real final screen... (using the built in font) and NOT the red/black color scheme. I went with black/green. I thought I had done brown... hmm... oh yea, ran out of colors to use, and the brown did not look good with the sea floor...

Anyway, that is some off the top of my head thoughts... If folks have questions, I'll try to answer...

7330:
Sorry the history was not clear.

History of Brett and Bally...

"Spectre Systems" (a company my friends and I started) had started writing programs for the TRS-80. Crunch Bug, Black Box, and others, but they were black and white and were not 'exciting'.

I love taking things apart and figuring out how they work. I bought a Bally arcade. I took it apart.

Since the Bally shared the same processor (Z-80) as the TRS-80, it was an easy jump for me to reverse engineer the Bally, and use the TRS-80 to disassemble the Bally's ROM and map out the software calls.

We used the TRS-80 as our assembler for the games. And once we started generating object code, we realized that if we mapped the Bally slot space into the TRS-80 Expansion memory map (and wired it up as such), we would have a 'real-time' development environment for the Bally Arcade. All we had to do was target the TRS-80 Expansion RAM space for the object code, hit reset on the Bally, and it would then 'execute' the code from the TRS-80 as if it were a cartridge. At the same time, the TRS-80 was still able to examine and change memory locations, so we could 'tweak' the parameters of the game on the fly.

I used that information I was gathering to start playing with assembly routines (a few of which were published in the Arcadian and Cursor magazines). Sprite tutorials, 3 tone music, etc... I figured out how to augment basic programs with assembler programs (not sure if I was the first, but I like to share what I found, mostly with the Michigan "BUG" group - Bally User Group).

I started playing with the light pen, and around that time figured out that the intercept register did not work the way that it seemed it should. So, I contacted Bally and was directed to Jeff Frederiksen. I explained that the intercept register did not seem to be working the way that I thought it should and I was confused. Jeff explained that there was a error in the silicon and the intercept register was broken. (well, partially broken, but I don't remember all the specific details, again, I'd have to go look at some code to remember all the details.)

Jeff was amazed that I had figured out that the register was broke. I explained that I had reversed engineered the chipset, that I had figured out how to program in assembly using the basic cart, and that I was now interfacing a light pen to the console using the light pen port.

Jeff invited me to Chicago (Dave Nutting Associates) to talk... So I went out and met the folks at DNA and got a tour of the facilities and we talked about hardware design, programming, cartridges, and more.

They wanted me to come program for them...

I was still going to UofM at the time, so I wanted to stay in school, but I was building a TRS-80 based development system for programming game cartridges. And I did. I suggested that I could do a game for them using the TRS-80. (the ICBM Attack proposal) They did not believe me, so I went ahead and created ICBM Attack. Then they believed me.

But they still were not set up to do remote programming. They were still building the development environment on the UV-1. So, I wrote Treasure Cove.

Later they started "Action Graphics" which Bob Ogden was going to head up to do cartridges for the arcade (some spin out deal from DNA). So, I got a DataMax UV-1 development system, and proceeded to try and learn the "Bally" way of developing cartridges. I did not do well. History of Brett and Bally...



"Spectre Systems" (a company my friends and I started) had started writing programs for the TRS-80. Crunch Bug, Black Box, and others, but they were black and white and were not 'exciting'.



I love taking things apart and figuring out how they work. I bought a Bally arcade. I took it apart.



Since the Bally shared the same processor (Z-80) as the TRS-80, it was an easy jump for me to reverse engineer the Bally, and use the TRS-80 to disassemble the Bally's ROM and map out the software calls.



We used the TRS-80 as our assembler for the games. And once we started generating object code, we realized that if we mapped the Bally slot space into the TRS-80 Expansion memory map (and wired it up as such), we would have a 'real-time' development environment for the Bally Arcade. All we had to do was target the TRS-80 Expansion RAM space for the object code, hit reset on the Bally, and it would then 'execute' the code from the TRS-80 as if it were a cartridge. At the same time, the TRS-80 was still able to examine and change memory locations, so we could 'tweak' the parameters of the game on the fly.



I used that information I was gathering to start playing with assembly routines (a few of which were published in the Arcadian and Cursor magazines). Sprite tutorials, 3 tone music, etc... I figured out how to augment basic programs with assembler programs (not sure if I was the first, but I like to share what I found, mostly with the Michigan "BUG" group - Bally User Group).



I started playing with the light pen, and around that time figured out that the intercept register did not work the way that it seemed it should. So, I contacted Bally and was directed to Jeff Frederiksen. I explained that the intercept register did not seem to be working the way that I thought it should and I was confused. Jeff explained that there was a error in the silicon and the intercept register was broken. (well, partially broken, but I don't remember all the specific details, again, I'd have to go look at some code to remember all the details.)



Jeff was amazed that I had figured out that the register was broke. I explained that I had reversed engineered the chipset, that I had figured out how to program in assembly using the basic cart, and that I was now interfacing a light pen to the console using the light pen port.



Jeff invited me to Chicago (Dave Nutting Associates) to talk... So I went out and met the folks at DNA and got a tour of the facilities and we talked about hardware design, programming, cartridges, and more.



They wanted me to come program for them...



I was still going to UofM at the time, so I wanted to stay in school, but I was building a TRS-80 based development system for programming game cartridges. And I did. I suggested that I could do a game for them using the TRS-80. (the ICBM Attack proposal) They did not believe me, so I went ahead and created ICBM Attack. Then they believed me.



But they still were not set up to do remote programming. They were still building the development environment on the UV-1. So, I wrote Treasure Cove.



Later they started "Action Graphics" which Bob Ogden was going to head up to do cartridges for the arcade (some spin out deal from DNA). So, I got a DataMax UV-1 development system, and proceeded to try and learn the "Bally" way of developing cartridges. I did not do well. While I'm very good at picking up languages, I did not do well with the TERSE environment (Grumble RPN, Grumble Bally framework, Grumble confusing instructions) and my first 'task' was to program "Defender", later released as Cosmic Raider. Sadly, I did not do well with the UV-1 and I returned the system and someone at Bally wrote the Cosmic Raider game (which they did very well with!).



Anyway, I graduated from UofM and had many offers from various companies, but Bally said they would match my best offer if I would come work for them. I did, but I actually ended up working for "Frederiksen and Shu Laboratories" . Bally had shut down the game development at DNA, and Jeff formed FSL with David Shu (who had built the UV-1 systems for him with his manufacturing company). At FSL we make cable scrambling systems, image processing systems for the NSA, an authoring system for early computer multimedia (before CDs and DVDs!), and much more... Eventually we created a digital video frame buffer (the Video Explorer) which was used in Broadcast Video (networks and post houses) and a company was spun off called "Intelligent Resources - Integrated Systems" which took the Video Explorer to market. We sold to Sony, Philips, 3DO, Minerva and many other companies. We were the engine used to bring video in to many media authoring/compressi on systems. Such
 as the Minerva Compressionist (DVDs), or Phillps VX-1 authoring/compressi on system (for CD-i Compact Disc interactive) , or 3DO for their games.

7341:
I received a package from Brett on Monday with information for me to scan and add to Ballyalley.com.  I've now scanned in (and uploaded) everything except for one document in that package over the past few days.  The last document to scan is the source-code for the game "Treasure Cove."

The "Treasure Cove" source-code is twenty-seven pages-- not too long.  Like many documents printed from "back in the day," the source code was sent to a printer and there are no page breaks, so the printout just covers each page from top to bottom.  On some of the pages the last line on a page covers some of the next page.  This makes scanning a little difficult, so this document will take me a little while to get right.

As Brett already mentioned, this source is short on comments.  The first three pages has plenty of comments, but then the comments get fewer and fewer.  Some pages have no comments at all.  Still, this source-code separates the graphics from the Z-80 mnemonics, which gives anyone disassembling a cartridge a HUGE headstart!

I'm not sure how much different this early version is from the finished release, but at some point in the future I'd like to take the "Treasure Cove" cartridge dump and recreate the source code in text format.  Using this not-yet-finished source will make that possible!

Thanks, Brett!

Adam

The reason that I'm making a distinction between the multicart version of Vipersoft BASIC and the version loaded from tape is that there is an advantage of loading from tape (believe it or not!).  The advantage is that it is loaded with AstroBASIC.  Since this is the case, the AstroBASIC 2000-BAUD interface can be used to load or save Vipersoft BASIC programs.  When Vipersoft BASIC is loaded from cartridge then it must use the 300-BAUD interface to save and load programs.

I'm not sure if there is a swapping method to exchange cartridge like there is with Bally BASIC and AstroBASIC.  Does anyone know?

I recently took care of one of my to-do's and contacted Dick Ainsworth to ask a few questions.  He'd made a couple of posts to the group in 2002, which are reprinted on Bally Alley:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ballyalley/interviews/dick_ainsworth.txt

I was particularly interested in more information about the Astrology cart he'd worked on, however.  I got some great details on that, along with further comments on Bingo Math, the BASIC Sampler tape, and the general view of the system by the Bally management.

With Dick's permission, I'm sending some of these on to the group.  I'll also point him this way in case he wants to participate in the discussion.  I've formatted it as an interview, but it's basically unedited.

Interview with Dick Ainsworth
by Paul Thacker
April 18, 2009 - April 21, 2009

Paul:  "One topic I always find fascinating is unreleased games.  You mentioned working on the planetarium program, which I take to be Astrology advertised in some flyers we have on-line.  If you don't mind satisfying my curiosity, what were your goals with this program?  How far along did it get, and why was it never released?  Do any prototypes or documents about it still exist?"

Dick:  "I designed the planetarium program as a small-scale model of the Adler in Chicago.  I hired a physics professor to work with me on developing the actual code that would drive the program.  The original idea was to project the Zodiac as a cylinder, which would fill the screen and move left or right, with the planets in the correct position for a real-time display of their actual position, or an for accurate view for any date.  This simplistic view would be accurate enough to represent a current night sky for viewing, and also provide a model for understanding how the universe works.  Unfortunately, the Bally folks wanted something that would tell fortunes "So people don't have to read that stuff in the newspaper".  I went ahead with my design, since Bally had no idea what we were doing, but the project was never completed."

Paul:  "Thanks for the info.  That helps explain why Astrology was advertised as being scientific/educational, along with the horoscope aspect.  Is there any chance that code or ROM's for the unfinished program still exists somewhere?  That would be quite a find."

Dick:  ""The planetarium project never made it into final code, though the preliminary equations worked fine.  None of this remains."

Paul:  "We've actually done a lot of work recently in archiving software and documents.  We've even got a dump of Color BASIC, now.  Have you held onto anything from that period?"

Dick:  "I have the listings for the original Bally BASIC software which came with the audio tape interface.  These are all programs I wrote.  [This has been archived.]  When I was recording this software for duplication on audio tape cassette, I met Bill Gates who was also at the same GRT studio, making a cassette of his BASIC.  As far as I know, it's a tossup as to which of these programs was the first production software for the personal computer.

If anyone has a VisualBASIC version of the original BallyBASIC, I would be delighted to know about it.  I would like to release my original BallyBASIC course, etc. in its original format, using VB to recreate the really cool Bally BOX, LINE, PLAY, etc..  See my computer seminar (in QuickBASIC) for a general idea.  It's on my personal page at www.qwerty.com.  I still think that a version of this language that could run on a modern Windows system would be great fun."

Paul:  "I do recognize some of the programs in your seminar, like Newtona 500.  I don't think anyone's tried a VisualBASIC implementation of Bally BASIC, however, though that would be cool to see.  There is a program called MESS that will emulate the system, and therefore run Bally BASIC on a modern PC, but unfortunately it doesn't have tape loading support yet."

Paul:  "Also, have you kept in touch with any of the other people at Bally?  There are many people we'd love to hear from."

Dick:  "Tom DeFanti who was an early player and developed a version of his ZGRASS language for the Astrocade is still a good friend.  We are currently collaborating on several projects.  Jay Fenton (now Jamie Fae Fenton) created the actual BallyBASIC language.  I haven't contacted Jay/Jamie in several years."

Paul:  "I recognize Tom DeFanti's name.  The expansion unit intended to run ZGRASS is sort of a holy grail among the Astrocade community.  It was never released, but supposedly some prototype units got out there.  I've never seen one, though.  I think Adam Trionfo, who runs the Bally Alley site, talked to Tom at some point, but I can ask if anyone has any questions for him."

Dick:  "At one time, Tom DeFanti and I shared a house in Oak Park, a suburb of Chicago.  At various times this house was also home to Jay Fenton, Larry Cuba (who created the first StarWars trench simulation on Tom's massive ZGRASS system at U of I), Ted Nelson, and others.  It's too bad that most of the "computer revolution" is thought of in terms of the west coast, when quite a bit of interesting development was going on in the midwest as well.

Bally is a strange contributor to the entire process of making computers available to people -- as opposed to governments, corporations, and universities.  Bally was the world's expert at extracting quarters from adults via slot machines.  When video games hit as coin-op systems, Bally/Midway became equally expert in extracting quarters from children.  They saw the Bally Arcade as simply a way of extracting lots of quarters all at once.  Bally never understood what computers were -- or the potential impact of actually owning one.  They refused to use the word "computer" in any of their advertising for the arcade because they thought it was too complicated.  They commissioned me to "create something that made it (the Arcade) look like it's educational"  Bingo Math was actually a revolution in program design -- the first educational software ever sold  -- the first "user modeling" system -- the first program to use interval timing, etc.  These innovations
 led directly to my creation of the first Typing Tutor, sold by Microsoft , IBM, etc.

Had Bally gone ahead with the first (and quite simply the best) computer system of it's time, using Tom's language, it could have been the computer that changed everything.  Instead, Bally decided to open another casino in Atlantic City.  And the rest is (or actually isn't) history."

Paul:  "Yes, one of the things I keep hearing from people is that the system was consistently mismanaged, by both Bally and Astrocade Inc."

Dick:  "I don't think Bally mismanaged the arcade, etc.  They never intended to make a "personal computer" at all.  They wanted to combine the best of the coin-op games in a box they could sell.  Which they did.  So they can't be faulted for not realizing the potential of a much greater opportunity.  At that time, the very idea of a personal computer sounded totally weird to anybody outside of the small group of folks who where actually involved in making the personal computer revolution happen.

I tried to explain to Bally the potential of what they had.  I even went before the Bally board of directors with an extensive presentation, showing that the ultimate game is learning to CREATE games.  I talked a lot about the incredible potential for people actually using the expanded Bally system for much more than a game box.  The Bally execs listened patiently, but ultimately decided to stick with things that they knew about.  Their next major move was to drop the computer idea and build a new casino in Atlantic City."

1) The planetarium program was a pretty big idea.  I wouldn't figure that it would be so complicated.

I added a picture of Mike White with Friends (from a July 4'th weekend, 1985) to Ballyalley.com. The people, all Astrocade folks, in order of appearance, from left to right, are: Leroy G. Flamm, Mike White, Don Gladden, and Tim White.

59400 Nine Mile Rd.
South Lyon, Mi.

I received a second package of material-to-scan from Brett Bilbrey today.  This one is full of stuff, some of which is already online at Ballyalley.com for sure, some of it MAY be online, and some of it DEFINITELY isn't!  I'm going to mention everything, even if some of it is online already.

1) Bally BASIC Source-Code (August 25, 1979) - There version is dated about 1 1/2 years prior to the one already online (which is actually AstroBASIC, even though it's labeled as Bally BASIC).  Perhaps this is the official Bally BASIC code (though it is dated later than the released cartridge)?  There are handwritten notes on some of the pages-- from Brett, I presume.  This would be a perfect opportunity to try my new document scanner when it gets here next week, but I'm pretty sure that this would jam the scanner... so on the flatbed scanner it will go!

2) Photograph of Unknown person with mustache in suit.  I'll scan this and see who Brett says it is.

3) Bally Fun and Brains catalog - Already online.

4) Three pages of information on the UV/1 in a colorful folder with screenshots of UV/1 artwork (the folder is already online, but the rest isn't).

5) Bally Professional Arcade Catalog, this one by Astrovision, Inc.  This seems similar to what is online... though it IS different.  It might be the first catalog by Astrovision... maybe.

6) Another Bally Professional Arcade Catalog by Astrovision, Inc.  It has several games, including games (with screenshots) for several unreleased games: Munchie, Coloring Book with Light Pen, Music Maker I, Quest for the Orb (Yup, it's the Conan that we know, but this one is probably more of an artist's imagination screenshot).

7) "It Starts with the Bally Computer System" catalog by Bally.  There goes Dick's thought that Bally wouldn't use the word computer.  I think this is already online.

8) "5 New Fun Cartridge for the Bally Professional Arcade by Astrovision."  This isn't online.  This catalog contains Galactic Invasion, Music Maker I, Space Fortress, Grand Derby / Demolition Derby, and Biorhythm.

9) Bally Professional Owner's Manual.  A B&W version of this manual that I've never seen before.  I guess this came with the original Arcade?  I bet there isn't a heat warning!

10) "Bally Professional Arcade Home TV Entertainment Center" leaflet.  I've not seen this either.  It has another multigeneration family (six of 'em!) having WAY too much fun together playing videogames!  Don't they know the Bally only has four controller ports?

11) An AstroVision, Inc. Business Card  - This one is for Rick Claghorn.  This is neat, as I've never seen one of these before.

12) Arcadian Reply Card

13) RMH Enterprises Reply Card

14) "Fact and Figures About the Bally Professional Arcade and Computer Add-On" - Pretty neat.  I don't think that this is online.

15) Bally Computer System - Video Console and Programming Keyboard - grayscale and color versions.  The grayscale version is already online, but the color version, I don't think, is.  The color on this picture is badly faded and off-color.

16) Picture of the Astrocade Standup Demonstration Unit.  This is B&W, but pretty cool!  I wonder if we'll ever get really good quality pictures of these.

17) Bally Computer System Specifications Video Console & Programming Keyboard. - The Bally directly compared against the Apple II, Commodore Pet, Compucolor Renaissance (the what!?!), Exidy Sorcerer, and the Radio Shack TRS-80 Level II.  Guess who wins!

18) Astrocade Full-Page B&W Ad from Leisure Time Electronics, January 1982

19) Arcade - Doesn't Just Play Games Ad - With 1982 TV Schedule Las Vegas market of commercials on back.  This is WEIRD.  There were commercials aired during the most popular shows of the time.  This give very specific air dates (including time of day).

20) Ad for "Astro Arcade BASIC"  Ever hear of THAT before?!?  How many names did BASIC for the Astrocade need!

21) Astrocade "The Professional Arcade"  - I think this is already online.

22) Bally Professional Arcade Expandable Computer System from Astrovision, Inc - Already online.

23) Bally Professional Arcade Expandable Computer System from Astrovision, Inc - This is different from above: there is a white Arcade on cover.  The inside seems similar or the same.

24) "You Love Us in the Arcades" Ad by Bally - I've CERTAINLY never seen THIS one before.  This one has a cool cutout on the cover... not sure how I'll scan this in properly.  There is a small "arcade" (as in, a place where people go to play games-- not the console) with three videogames (Checkmate, Gunfight and Tornado Baseball).  When you open the front page, you'll see that the videoscreen for the arcade game Gunfight is actually coming from the Bally Professional Arcade.  The "screenshots" inside for Checkmate, Gunfight and Calculator are done by magic marker, I think.  I'd love to see the original of these.  Who drew stuff like this?  This one is pretty different, that's for sure.

25) Graph Paper for Astrocade - This is online... but there seem to be some additional ones that might not be online yet.  Brett, I know that these were available for sale.  Did they sell much?


I'm separating the additional items into a different section, as it's all material for or by Brett and/or Spectre Systems.  I'll need more information about almost all of this!

1) BASIC/ML Program - Program by Brett .  I THINK that this is Critter.  Was this the version sent into the Arcadian for print?

2) Program Ideas (11-8-82) - Thirty game ideas!  One is called "Under Sea Game (Octopus's Garden).  Is this the germ for Treasure Cove?!?

3) Beaver Dam Game Info - Five pages of pretty well laid-out work, including a cute color beaver graphic.  This is, by far, the furthest any of the game ideas seemed to go.

4) Unicorn Game - Four pages about "Gregory the Cross-Eyes Unicorn."

5) Battle Cry - One page.  This is the Battlezone game that Brett made reference to a couple of weeks ago.

6) Astro-Bots - Not more than 1/3 a page about this.

7) Space War - This game looks like the TV was going to have to be put on its side to play vertically!  Any thoughts on this, Brett?

8) Maze Notes - Some sort of maze notes on graph paper.

9) Duck Range on Graph Paper - A hunter in one corner and ducks fly overhead.  This remind me of  Dog Patch, but you just shoot ducks-- thatâs how the screen layout looks, anyway.

10) Tail Gunner Outline - About half a page of notes.

11) Star Wars - Game Outline with graphics on notepaper.

12) Suggestions for Conan - This one made me laugh!  At the top is says, "this would be better than what was at the show!" There is a page full of ideas on how to make Conan a better game.

13) The Music Program - The Compiler - These directions start on page 13.  I'm not exactly sure that this is related to the Astrocade.  Brett, do you know what this is?  Maybe I'll scan it and it will refresh your memory.  Perhaps this was to some Radio Shack program?

14) Logo Designs for Spectre Systems - Eight pages of potential Logos for Spectre Systems.  I like this!

15) Spectre Systems Handle Ad - I didn't know that these were available for sale without the game.  Interestingly, the handles could be customized!

16) Bally / Astrocade Graphics Design Pads Ad

17) Battle Space Idea - 1/3 of a page idea for a game

18)  Three Index Cards - I think this is a list of the games that Brett had on tapeâ¦

19) Nine-Page Letter to "Bob and Scot" from Brett (3/24/72) - This letter was sent, as this is a photocopy of the original letter.  It talks about the seven games: Battle Cry, Astro Bots, Astro Attack, Mazeway, ICBM Attack, Lunar Base, and Lone Rover.  Each game has a description with a hand-drawn "screenshot."  Pretty neat.  Brett, is this when you were trying to interest Bally or Astrovision in your work?


That's the extent of what was sent to me.  Thanks for making this available for me to scan, and share with the group, Brett!  I'll start scanning this stuff soon (next week, I hope).  In the meantime, I'm actually going to be working on the website, catching up with stuff that's on my hard drive but not online.

Adam

I added "Using the AstroBASIC 2000-BAUD Interface with Vipersoft BASIC," by Lance Squire, to Ballyalley.com.

This documentation discusses swapping AstroBASIC with Vipersoft BASIC loaded into RAM, either from a multicart, a cartridge created from an EPROM or from (probably the most common method) loading Vipersoft BASIC from a tape.  This cartridge swap is done so that the AstroBASIC tape interface can be used to save or load to tape at the faster 2000-BAUD instead of requiring the much slower (and rarer!) 300-BAUD external interface.

I want to thank everyone for being so helpful on this topic. I wanted to give you all an update, and let you know that I decided to send my Astrocade to the folks at Atari2600.com to have the RF shielding removed. They did a fantastic job, and the unit came back to me last week. I was able to play it for an hour without any problems, which was a great improvement since when I first bought the unit, I couldn't even run it for more than 5 minutes without it overheating.

Thank you Lance for your instructions on how to remove the shielding since that is what the technicians used to get the job done.

Since it was my first time ever playing the system, I thought I'd share my impressions. First off, I think the console looks really cool. Definitely looks like something straight out of the 70s. The controllers are the most comfortable I used for any classic console, and I like that they're ambidextrous. I only have one game so far - Astro Battle - and I'm really impressed with it. The graphics and sound are very good for something of that era, and I'm just hooked on the console. The only thing keeping me from playing it for longer periods, is lack of time.

Thank you for all your help, and I look forward to expanding my Astrocade knowledge and having fun!

Jose

1) Verify that it works, period.  Powered on and can play games, and for more than 5 minutes.  That's key to it being worth any real $$$.  I've been collecting Bally systems for over nine years and I can tell you working vs. untested, unplayed or "I can't connect it to my TV" makes a big difference on what it's worth. 

2) Pictures, and lots of them.  Just because they say it's unplayed doesn't mean it's not scratched.  Looks for them on the cartridge bay cover, cracks as well.  Worn gold trim around the console base, buttons etc., controllers too (just the Bally imprinted ones, some of the later controllers no longer had the name so they must have changed the mold).  So physical condition plays a big part too. 

3) Nameplate variations/different models, which I would say revolves around which is the most rare or most desirable.  My ratings from highest to lowest value:

1) Home Library Computer
2) Bally Professional Arcade (Montgomery Ward version, also know as the "White" console).
3) Astrocade
4 Bally Professional Arcade (standard black/wood-grain console).
5) Bally Computer system.

I would rate the Home Library computer as the most valuable/collectible.  Holy grail, Ark of the covenant, etc.  They don't come up for sale that often, and a working one is about as rare as they come (AFAIK, I have the only working HLC version known to exist). 

Next comes a tie between the White Montgomery Ward BPA and the Astrocade labeled console.  Note that the White console should have the correct matching BPA cartridge port cover with a small MW label on the cover, and the Astrocade labeled console should have a silver bottom label with blue writing.  Although at one time I would have rated the Astrocade labeled console more rare and more valuable, I have now seen a pretty somewhat equal number of the two console type come up for sale within the past few years (at one time I had even questioned if the Astrocade labeled consoles were ever produced, but now have two in my collection). 

The Bally Professional Arcade would come next, followed by the Bally Computer System model.  I find much more of the BCS come up for sale hence I would value it the least. 

Note: I consider the "black" Montgomery Ward BPA consoles a variation only, and only slightly in value than a "regular" BPA, if anything at all.  I don't really consider it a separate model, which is why I didn't list it as such.

You can view some excellent examples from our own Glankonian here:

http://www.glankonian.com/~lance/Unit%20Labels.html

And here:

http://www.glankonian.com/~lance/Unit%20Bottom%20Labels.html

As far as prices go (and it's really what you want to know) I have paid as little as $29.00 dollars to as much as $200.00 for a console, so use your best judgment.  Keep in mind a bundled auction for a Bally can often have hidden treasures, like copies of rare games (Blast Droids, Treasure Cove) or prototypes (Munchie), or even accessories like the Bally Steering Wheel for 280 Zzzap/Dodgem (now 9 wheels known to exist in the world).  So keep that in mind if you are looking at something for sale.

-Michael

Adam-

I tend to agree with Bill's comments on this, and $10 probably isn't all that much for part of a homebrew package.  I'm guessing more like a 50 - 100 or more cart run would have brought the cost down, but like we all know we aren't dealing with the same numbers in collectors as with other systems.  (And Bill, forget Pac-Man, you don't want to know what I paid for an original Protector for the Vectrex, and it wasn't what Alex Hebert sold them for!).

I think Toby's idea is good to, with the boxed, labeled and instructions carts being the "limited edition" ones, and you can always make just plain carts on-demand down the road, provided there are any cart kits left (it would be great for someone like 8bitDomain to come up with a new cartridge board and chip to replace the old design).  I would suggest though that any "standard" or "no frills" carts get something to differentiate them from the LE ones, like a different label.  I would also suggest numbering the LE carts 1 - 25, or 1 of 25, 2 of 25 etc.

Try this guy as well: www.UncleTusk.com for boxes, maybe he can help.  Got his name off the back of an NES cart I just picked up called "Happy Camper" from NGD:

http://nationalgamedepot.zoomshare.com/0.html

Has to be the best homebrew box I have seen to date, even feels like something right off the shelf from Gamestop.  Better than the boxes from OPCODE, Atari2600 etc.

Anyway, www.UnlceTusk.com is credited with the box design. 

By the way, did Mike White ever get rid of the hundreds of cart shells he had up for sale?  With a new board design I think you might lure those other Bally homebrew programmers into completing their games...

-Michael

7475:
Lance-

Nobody is out of any running, trust me.  Like I said I just haven't gotten around to deciding what I wanted to do with them.  At least three of them would be part of a set for each Bally I have on display, which right now is only two of three consoles: a Montgomery Ward White and an Astrocade.  I want to clean the Home Library Computer model up a bit more professionally before I put it out.

And by set I mean to "complete" each Bally so to speak, with controllers 1- 4, the Bally switchbox (tough to find), all documents, original BASIC cart and modem for the HLC and probably the white console (anybody know the time frame on when those were sold by Montgomery Ward?) and the Astorcade BASIC for the Astrocade.  These are things I have been planning for a while now, but just haven't had the time or been able to make any. 

There is a very good chance that I would consider unloading a good portion of my other items, which although I consider of value to me are not really what I intended to collect but wound up acquiring anyway.  Possible items would be all the chips (RAM, CPU etc.) and related console spare parts, spare controllers and related spare parts, a number of spare consoles in various states and yes, even the BalCheck could be up for grabs.

Although it's probably what I consider to be the most rare item in my collection (it's the only BalCheck I know to exist, anywhere; not to be confused with the two Ballycheck tester devices from RGB Electronics that Adam has) there really isn't much for me to do with it.  It's not pretty (there are pics on the ballyalley site) and would really only benefit the die-hard collector who has to have everything, or someone who can actually use it to diagnose and fix consoles.  Better yet, find a way to reverse engineer it and come up with a modern day equivalent and then sell it to the masses at a decent price. 

Anyway, I'm out for three weeks come May and will be setting aside at least one day as a "Bally" day to take inventory, pics etc. to fulfill a bunch of requests and such.  From there I will have a better idea of what I plan to do with everything and will let the group know.  If anyone is visiting Long Island in late May or early June and wants to stop by and check everything out, take their own pics or just play around with some vintage stuff, just drop me a line. 

Swing set should be up by then, but that just for my kids, sorry.

-Michael

That's true--even now we're not sure what to call it.  Really, there was never a "Bally Astrocade," since Bally marketed it as the Bally Professional Arcade (or perhaps the Bally Computer System, or the Home Library Arcade).  Astrovision later settled on the Astrocade name, at first using the Bally name to market it, then dropping that entirely when they no longer had the rights to do so.  It's harder to remember a machine if you hear five different names for it instead of something consistent like Intellivision, or Vectrex.

Paul

I never liked it called the "Bally Astrocade" because as noted there is no such thing.

However, all names before the change to "Astrocade" were proceeded with "Bally".

Bally|Home Library Computer, Bally|Professional Arcade,
Bally|Computer System

Astrovision just used the previous Bally labels until there right to use it ran out.

It looks like they wanted to for with Astro|Professional Arcade.

However, the reasons for the corporate name change seem to also have forced a change in system name to: Astrocade. Though it looks like they tried to go with Astrocade|The Professional Arcade as seen on the boxes.

As we know when they ran out of Astrocade labels, they used the existing stock of Bally labels, but the boxes and marketing all said Astrocade. Further leading to confusion no doubt.

I personally prefer Bally/Astrocade the '/' being and 'and/or' type thing, noting the companies that sold it.

Of course, If I wanted to be complete Bally/Astrovision/Astrocade, but the last two are really the same.
